newsitem.title: USA: Black syphilis study victims to get Clinton apology.
newsitem.headline: Black syphilis study victims to get Clinton apology.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Friday prepared to apologise officially on behalf of the government to a group of black men whose syphilis went untreated for decades as part of a U.S. Public Health Service study.

Five of the eight living survivors of the U.S. Public Health Service study, which began in Tuskegee, Alabama, in 1932 and lasted for 40 years, travelled to Washington for the White House ceremony. The others were too ill to participate.
Herman Shaw, 94, who was part of the group, was asked to introduce the president at the East Room ceremony.

The government medical experiment involved 400 black men who were left untreated for syphilis for 40 years to allow doctors to study the course of the disease, even though antibiotic treatment was available.
Survivors shared in a $10 million compensation award made by the government in 1974, but there has never been a formal apology until now.
"This was an extraordinary episode in the history of our country and a real blight on the record of the United States government," White House spokesman Mike McCurry said.

"It has been dealt with in the technical, legal sense that there has been compensation -- recompense for those who are victims," McCurry said. "But there has never been the formal apology that the president believes is deserved in this case."

The spokesman said Clinton would also offer some specific ideas "on things that we can do to address in general the question of proper funding and proper accountability for federally funded medical research."

Clinton's apology is not unprecedented. He previously expressed regret to Americans who unknowingly served as guinea pigs in government radiation experiments that took place years before he became president.
His effort to make amends for the Tuskegee experiment was part of a series of events aimed at breaking down racial barriers set to take place over the next month.

"I think this fits into a pattern of things that the president has perceived this year that really talk about how we can come together as a very diverse country that should celebrate its racial ethnic diversity, and use that as an element of our strength," McCurry said.

Dr. Randell Morgan, president of the predominantly black National Medical Association, said Clinton's apology did not excuse the Tuskegee study "but it may help close this unfortunate chapter in our nation's history."

"The legacy of this horrible experiment, which lasted 40 years, continues to affect African-Americans today and has led to a sense of fear and general mistrust of the medical research process and the scientific community," Morgan said.
